topic.title: Loops in C
topic.description: for, while and do-while: how a loop actually evaluates, how to pick the right one, and the four bugs that cost more marks than any other topic in C.

curriculum.summary: A loop is one idea: do a thing again until a condition stops being true. C gives you three spellings of it, and they are not equally good. This topic teaches the evaluation order of `for` (the part everyone gets wrong), how to choose between the three forms, how to avoid off-by-one errors by deciding the range *before* you write the loop, and how `scanf` and loops interact — the single most common source of "my program skips my input" bugs.

rules.commentPolicy: Every non-obvious line needs a WHY comment, not a WHAT comment. A comment that restates the code is deleted. A comment that states the reason is kept.
rules.notePolicy: Write three lines maximum: what you learned, what broke, what is next. If it needs more than 220 characters per line, it is not understood yet.

explanation.h: 2. The three forms, and when each is right
explanation.md:
C has exactly three loops. They are the same idea in different clothes.

| Form | Shape | Idiomatic when |
|---|---|---|
| `for` | init; test; step | the number of iterations is known or computable up front |
| `while` | test only | the loop runs until something changes that you did not count |
| `do...while` | body first, test after | the body must run **at least once** |

**The rule of thumb:** if you can write the count down before the loop starts, use `for`. If you genuinely cannot, use `while`. Use `do...while` only when "at least once" is part of the requirement — menu loops, input validation, and reading until EOF.

`while` is not the "beginner" version of `for`. It is the *honest* version: it says "I do not know how many times yet", and that is a real and common situation.

explanation.h: 3. The four parts of a for loop — and the exact order they run
4. A for loop is just a while loop in disguise
5. Off-by-one: decide the range before you write the loop
explanation.md:
The single most common bug in beginner C is being off by exactly one. It happens because the boundary is decided *while writing the loop*, at the moment you are least focused.

**Decide the range in English first, then translate it.**

| The English | The C | Common mistake |
|---|---|---|
| "from 1 to n, both included" | `i = 1; i <= n; i++` | writing `i < n` and dropping `n` |
| "the first n items, 0-indexed" | `i = 0; i < n; i++` | writing `i <= n` and reading one past the end |
| "from 0 to n-1 inclusive" | `i = 0; i < n; i++` | — |

Two habits kill the bug:

1. **Write the range as a comment on the line above the loop**, in English: `/* i runs 1..n inclusive */`.
2. **Print the boundaries once** while testing: `printf("first=%d last=%d\n", i_first, i_last);`

Note the asymmetry that trips people up: `i <= n` and `i < n` are *both* correct — for different ranges. The bug is not using `<=`; the bug is using it **without deciding which range you meant**.

The genuinely dangerous case is `i <= n` on an **array**, because `array[n]` is one past the last valid element. There, `i < n` is not a style choice, it is memory safety.

explanation.h: 8. The scanf trap — why your loop skips input
9. Infinite loops, and breaking out on purpose
explanation.md:
An infinite loop is not always a bug.

```c
for (;;) {                 /* the idiomatic "forever" in C */
    char line[100];
    if (!fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin)) break;   /* EOF ends it */
    if (line[0] == 'q') break;
    process(line);
}
```

Three notes:

- `for (;;)` has all three parts **empty**, which is legal and means *forever*. `while (1)` does the same thing and is more readable to beginners.
- The **exit condition** should be at the top, checked before the work. That way the loop cannot do one iteration too many.
- A loop that reads input must handle **EOF** (`fgets` returns `NULL`), or it will spin forever on a closed pipe.

If your loop *should* terminate and does not, look at the step: `i++` missing, `i` never changing, or the condition comparing the wrong thing.

explanation.h: 10. The four bugs to check for
explanation.md:
When a loop misbehaves, check these in order:

1. **Off-by-one.** Is the boundary `<` or `<=` — and did you *decide* which range you meant?
2. **The step is missing or wrong.** `i++` vs `i += 2` vs `i = i + 1`.
3. **The accumulator is reset inside the loop.** `sum = 0` inside the body means every iteration starts from zero — the classic cause of "the answer is always the last number". Initialise **before** the loop.
4. **The input is never consumed.** The `scanf` trap from section 8 — a loop that reads but never advances, so the same value is read forever.

A fifth, for the curious: **integer overflow in the step**. `i++` on an `int` that has reached `INT_MAX` is undefined behaviour. It is not your problem today, but it is why `long long` exists for factorials.

videos.title: For Loop in C Programming (With Examples for Beginners)
videos.why: The shortest path to for-loop muscle memory. Watch this one first — it covers init/test/step without ever naming them, which is exactly how you should meet them.

videos.title: Loops in C | 4 Important C Programs + Scenario Based Problem
videos.why: Scenario-based, which is how loops actually get asked. The four programs here (table, factorial, sum, reverse) are the exact shapes of six of the tasks in this topic.

videos.title: Loops in One Shot
videos.why: One continuous pass over for, while and do-while. Use it to revise and to see the three side by side — not to learn from scratch.

videos.title: Jenny's Lectures — Programming in C (loops are lectures 33 to 45)
videos.why: The reference. Thirteen consecutive lectures covering loops, break, continue, nested loops, and while/do-while separately. This is the syllabus, in order, with Indian exam framing.

videos.title: C_34 For loop in C | C Programming Tutorials
videos.why: Single lecture, no playlist hunting. Use it as the direct substitute for the for-loop lectures if you only have twenty minutes.

videos.title: While Loop in C — GeeksforGeeks
videos.why: Not a video — a clean step-by-step of the evaluation order in pictures. Read it after the videos, not before, so you have a frame to hang it on.

references.why: Best text reference for the two loop forms the videos tend to gloss over. Small, example-heavy, no sign-up wall.

tasks.title: Print 1 to N
tasks.prompt: Read one integer N from stdin. Print the integers 1 through N on a single line, separated by one space. If N is 1, print `1`.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY the loop starts at 1 and not at 0.
hints: Print the number, then print a space only if it is not the last one.
The boundary decision: does your range include N? Write that down in English first.

tasks.title: Factorial of N
tasks.prompt: Read one integer N. Print N! (the product of 1..N). Define 0! as 1. Use `long long` so the answer stays correct up to 20.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY the accumulator starts at 1 and not at 0, and why the boundary includes N.
hints: The accumulator must be initialised before the loop, not inside it.
Think about what happens to the product if you ever multiply by zero.

tasks.title: Sum of digits
tasks.prompt: Read one non-negative integer N. Print the sum of its digits. For example, 1234 gives 10.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY you take the remainder before dividing.
hints: The last digit of a number is n % 10. The rest of the number is n / 10.
Order matters: take the remainder first, or you will divide away the digit you wanted.

tasks.title: Reverse a number
tasks.prompt: Read one non-negative integer N. Print N with its digits reversed. Leading zeros in the result are dropped: 120 becomes 21.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY the accumulator is `rev * 10 + digit` and not `rev + digit`.
hints: You build the answer from the right. Each new digit goes on the left of what you have.
rev * 10 shifts the existing digits left by one place, then you add the new digit.

tasks.title: FizzBuzz
tasks.prompt: Read one integer N. For each number from 1 to N print one line: `Fizz` if it is divisible by 3, `Buzz` if by 5, `FizzBuzz` if by both, otherwise the number itself.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY you test divisibility by 15 (or check FizzBuzz first) instead of testing 3 and 5 independently.
hints: If you test 3 first and print Fizz, you can never print FizzBuzz.
15 is divisible by both 3 and 5 — one test covers both.

tests.stdout:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz

tasks.title: Multiplication table
tasks.prompt: Read one integer N (1 to 10). Print the multiples of N from N×1 to N×10, separated by one space.
tasks.explainTarget: Your comment must state WHY the counter runs 1..10 rather than 0..9.
hints: You need ten multiples. Decide whether the counter is the multiple itself or the index.
There is more than one correct shape here — pick one and defend it in a comment.

written.q: When is a for-loop better than a while-loop?
written.a: Use for when the number of iterations is known or computable up front; use while when it is not known in advance.
written.partial: Mentions that the count is known in advance.

written.q: What is an off-by-one error and how do you avoid it?
written.a: The loop boundary includes or excludes one element too many or too few. Avoid it by deciding the range in English before writing the loop, then writing that range as a comment.
written.partial: Names the boundary/range as the thing that must be decided first.

written.q: Inside a for-loop, where does `continue` jump to?
written.a: It jumps to the step expression (the increment), not back to the condition — so the loop still terminates.
written.partial: Says it goes to the increment/step rather than the condition.

written.q: Why must an accumulator be initialised before the loop and not inside it?
written.a: Initialising inside the body resets it on every iteration, so each iteration overwrites the previous total and the final value is just the last iteration's contribution.
written.partial: Says it is reset each iteration.
